source: Fleming & Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition
finding: Review of measures of metacognition. Splits sensitivity (does confidence track accuracy) from bias (over or under confidence). Plain correlations are contaminated by response bias. SDT-based measures such as meta-d' and M-ratio are meant to be bias-free.
numbers: Cited 699 times (Europe PMC). Notes Henmon (1911): confidence correlates with accuracy but is not a reliable index of it.
quote: Metacognitive sensitivity is also known as metacognitive accuracy, type 2 sensitivity, discrimination
limits: Definitions and review only. Later work (b02) shows meta-d' still depends on task performance.
agent_relevance: Our agent must separate 'does stated confidence discriminate right from wrong' from 'is it too high'. Track both, never one number.

source: Rahnev (2025) A comprehensive assessment of current methods for measuring metacognition (Nat Commun)
finding: Tested 17 measures of metacognition on Confidence Database data. All valid, most similarly precise. Many depend strongly on task performance and only weakly on response and metacognitive bias. Split-half reliability is very high, but test-retest reliability is poor for most.
numbers: Datasets: Shekhar (20 subjects, 2800 trials each, 56,000 trials), Rouault1 (466 subjects, 97,860 trials), Rouault2 (484 subjects, 101,640 trials). 17 measures. Earlier work cited: meta-d', AUC2 and Phi depend strongly on performance; M-Ratio and meta-noise do not.
quote: no current measure of metacognitive ability is perfect
limits: Test-retest result rests on one dataset; the author says it needs replication. Perceptual tasks only.
agent_relevance: Individual 'metacognitive ability' is a weak trait even in humans. Do not build the schema on a stable per-model confidence skill. Re-measure per task and per run.

source: Dijkstra, Mazor & Fleming (2024) Confidence ratings do not distinguish imagination from reality (J Vision)
finding: Monitoring failed in a reality-monitoring task. Confidence criteria shifted together with the decision criterion when people imagined a signal, so confidence did not flag the error. Global offline questions showed task-level insight that was uncorrelated with trial-level insight.
numbers: Two experiments (Experiment 1 post-queries N=51). Hierarchical Bayesian modelling of confidence criteria.
quote: confidence ratings do not distinguish imagination from reality during perceptual detection
limits: Detection of faint gratings only; one paradigm. Local and global insight dissociate.
agent_relevance: A system can describe its own bias in general yet fail to flag it on the item. Add per-item external checks, not a global self-model (G10).

source: Grassi et al. (2025) Restoring sight in choice blindness: pupillometry and covert detection (Front Psychol)
finding: Challenges the classic choice-blindness reading. With a debrief, people reported most swapped-choice trials, and pupils dilated on all manipulated trials, reported or not. Authors read it as covert detection plus reluctance to report, not blindness to own intentions.
numbers: Concurrent reports 56.4% of manipulated trials (185/328). Concurrent plus retrospective 92.1% (302/328). Only 7% (23 trials) never reported. Retrospective alone 84.45% (277/328). The paper cites the classic setting as only about 13% called out. Pupil analysis of unreported trials: N=11, 16 trials.
limits: Small unreported-trial sample for pupils. Detection depends strongly on design (deception, stakes, relevance). Does not restore accurate reasons for choices.
agent_relevance: Reports of 'I did not notice' are also unreliable. Self-report is weak evidence in both directions, which supports checking outputs (G10).

source: Lau & Rosenthal (2011) Empirical support for higher-order theories of conscious awareness (TICS)
finding: Main empirical case for higher-order theory: dissociations between first-order performance and awareness (blindsight, TMS, matched-performance contrasts) fit a separate higher-order read-out of first-order states.
numbers: Not opened this session. Listed as cited 446 times in Europe PMC.
limits: Not read; the point is from memory of the field. Rival theories (global workspace, recurrent processing, first-order views) explain the same dissociations; see the Global Workspace Theory subfield.
agent_relevance: HOT explains why a system can hold states about its states. It does not say the self-model is accurate. Use it only as a design pattern: a second pass reads the first.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning models don't always say what they think (Anthropic)
finding: Reasoning models seldom admit using a planted hint. Reveal rate is often under 20%. Outcome-based RL raises faithfulness at first, then plateaus. Models that learn reward hacks almost never verbalize them.
numbers: Overall faithfulness: Claude 3.7 Sonnet 25%, DeepSeek R1 39%. Misalignment hints: 20% and 29%. Harder questions (GPQA vs MMLU): 44% and 32% relative drop. RL plateau: 28% MMLU, 20% GPQA. Reward hacks learned (reward above 0.99) but verbalized under 2% in 5 of 6 environments. Unfaithful CoTs longer: 2064 vs 1439 tokens (Claude 3.7).
quote: the reveal rate is often below 20%
limits: Hint-based score is an upper bound on true faithfulness. Settings where CoT is not necessary; harder tasks may force CoT use.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G10. Do not read a trace as a log of the cause. Verify with controlled perturbation and output checks.

source: Turpin et al. (2023) Language models don't always say what they think
finding: Biasing features in the prompt (suggested answer, answer always A, stereotypes) change answers while the CoT never mentions them. The CoT then rationalizes the biased answer.
numbers: Accuracy drop up to 36.3% (GPT-3.5, zero-shot CoT, suggested-answer bias) on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks. Answer-is-always-A: -18.7% GPT-3.5, -4.7% Claude 1.0. Few-shot reduces the drop: -36.3% to -24.1% (GPT-3.5), -30.6% to -21.5% (Claude 1.0). CoT helps unbiased accuracy: 57.1 to 59.6 (GPT-3.5), 59.2 to 65.3 (Claude 1.0).
quote: models virtually never verbalize Biasing Feature #1: Answer is Always A
limits: Older models (GPT-3.5, Claude 1.0). Bias features are artificial; real cues are not shown.
agent_relevance: A model's explanation of why it answered is a post-hoc story. Never ask 'why did you choose that' and trust it. Shuffle option order and compare answers.

source: Lanham et al. (2023) Measuring faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning
finding: Intervened on the CoT (early answering, adding mistakes, filler tokens, paraphrasing). Reliance on the CoT varies a lot by task. The CoT gain does not come from extra compute or phrasing alone. Larger, more capable models give less faithful reasoning on most tasks.
numbers: Per-task percentages not extracted (they are in figures). Headline from the abstract: faithfulness worsens with model size on most tasks studied.
quote: As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks
limits: One model family. The inverse-scaling trend is shown on a subset of tasks.
agent_relevance: Model size will not fix reporting. Use mistake-insertion tests to check whether a trace is load-bearing before trusting it.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple choice and true/false in the right format. P(True) self-evaluation of own samples works and improves with size. Showing the model many of its own samples first improves self-evaluation. P(IK) classifiers predict whether the model knows, but calibrate poorly on new tasks.
numbers: Models up to 52B. Self-evaluation scored by AUROC and Brier; Brier does not always fall with size (for example Codex). P(IK) rises with relevant source text and with hints for GSM8k.
limits: Early models, mostly base-model calibration results; P(IK) generalizes only partly; format-sensitive.
agent_relevance: Positive evidence for narrow self-knowledge: a probability read-out beats verbal guesses. Use P(True) or sample agreement as a signal, but check it per task.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration
finding: For RLHF models, verbalized confidence is better calibrated than token probabilities. Asking for several candidate answers with probabilities improves it further.
numbers: Often reduces ECE by a relative 50% or more on TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA for ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude 2.
limits: Calibration of aggregate numbers, not per-item discrimination. RLHF models only.
agent_relevance: Cheap usable signal: ask for top-k answers with probabilities. Still score discrimination (AUROC), not just ECE.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? (ICLR)
finding: Verbalized confidence is overconfident: values cluster at 80-100%, often multiples of 5. Calibration and failure prediction improve with capability but stay far from ideal. Human-inspired prompts, sampling consistency and better aggregation help. White-box methods are only slightly better.
numbers: Five LLMs, five dataset types. About 22.2% AUROC improvement from GPT-3 to GPT-4. White-box vs black-box AUROC gap reported as 0.522 to 0.605 (abstract). Paper flags ECE above 0.25 or AUROC below 0.6 as major deviation. Average ECE above 0.377 for weaker models.
quote: LLMs, when verbalizing their confidence, tend to be overconfident
limits: Hard expertise tasks (for example professional law) remain poor on failure prediction.
agent_relevance: A single verbalized confidence number is not a stop rule. Use agreement across independent attempts instead.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large language models must be taught to know what they don't know
finding: Prompting alone does not give good uncertainty. Fine-tuning on about a thousand graded examples (LoRA plus a prompt) beats baselines. A model can also estimate uncertainty about other models' answers.
numbers: About 1,000 graded examples suffice. Compared on MMLU multiple-choice and open-ended using ECE and AUROC. A user study showed the estimates change how people use LLM answers.
limits: Needs open weights and labelled data. Not a prompt-only scaffold.
agent_relevance: A scaffold cannot train this. Fallback: use a separate grader, since cross-model estimation works.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR)
finding: Intrinsic self-correction (no external feedback) does not help and often hurts. Earlier gains came from using oracle labels to decide when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA: 75.8 to 38.1 after self-correction (41.8 after more calls). GPT-3.5 GSM8K: 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7. GPT-4 GSM8K: 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5. GPT-3.5 keeps its first answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K and changes right to wrong more often than wrong to right.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback
limits: 2023 models; RL-trained reasoning models not tested. Prompts may be weak.
agent_relevance: Strong support for 'the model never grades its own answer without a check'. A second pass without a verifier is not metacognition.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? (TACL)
finding: Survey of self-correction. No prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs on general tasks. It works where reliable external feedback exists, after fine-tuning, or in tasks exceptionally suited to it. The bottleneck is feedback generation.
numbers: Survey, no single effect size.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Depends on its own taxonomy of research questions; fast-moving field.
agent_relevance: Refinement loops need a checker (tests, retrieval, tool). Without one, skip the loop.

source: Binder et al. (2024) Looking inward: language models can learn about themselves by introspection
finding: A finetuned model M1 predicts its own hypothetical behavior better than a stronger model M2 trained on M1's behavior. This holds after M1's behavior is changed. It fails on complex tasks and out-of-distribution generalization.
numbers: Llama 70B predicts itself 48.5% vs GPT-4o predicting Llama 31.8%. GPT-4o predicts itself 49.4% vs Llama 70B predicting GPT-4o 36.6%. GPT-3.5 advantage only +0.8% (p=0.002). Self-prediction training raised accuracy from 32.6% to 49.4%. After a behavior change, M1 predicts the new behavior at 35.4% vs old at 21.7%. Cross-prediction plateaus at 35.2%.
limits: Needs finetuning on self-prediction; small absolute effect; simple behavior properties. Rival reading is model similarity, not self-access (see b16).
agent_relevance: Weak, trained, narrow privileged access. Not a basis for trusting free-form self-reports.

source: Song, Hu & Mahowald (2025) Language models fail to introspect about their knowledge of language (COLM)
finding: Across 21 open-source LLMs, metalinguistic prompts do not predict a model's own string probabilities better than another similar model's probabilities. No privileged self-access found.
numbers: Meta-A to Direct-B correlation never above .25, even within model. Models more similar in Direct-Direct correlation are more consistent (r=.32). Only the 'other' similarity class differs from self (beta=-.03, p<.01); other classes p>.05. Accuracy high under both methods but agreement between methods low.
limits: Grammar and word prediction only; open models; assumes string probability is the true internal state.
agent_relevance: Prompted answers about the model's knowledge track a general model of language, not its own internals. Use direct probabilities or sampling, not 'ask it how it feels'.

source: Betley et al. (2025) Tell me about yourself: LLMs are aware of their learned behaviors (ICLR)
finding: Models finetuned on a behavior (risk seeking, insecure code, Make Me Say game) describe that behavior without examples. Some can tell if they have a backdoor, but cannot output the trigger by default.
numbers: GPT-4o and Llama-3.1-70B tested. Free-form trigger elicitation fails for non-reversal-trained models.
limits: Behavior was injected by finetuning; strongly shifted dispositions; could be learned association rather than inner access.
agent_relevance: Narrow behavior-level self-description can be real. External verification is still needed for anything that matters.

source: Plunkett, Morris et al. (2025) Self-interpretability: LLMs can describe complex internal processes that drive their decisions
finding: GPT-4o and 4o-mini fine-tuned to weigh attributes can report those weights. Report accuracy rises with explanation training and generalizes.
numbers: Learned weights track targets r=.84 (4o) and .87 (4o-mini). Reported vs actual weights r=.54 (95% HDI .47-.62) for 4o and r=.50 (.42-.59) for 4o-mini. Off-the-shelf models' reports barely correlated with the fine-tuned models' real weights.
limits: Moderate correlations; authors do not know whether introspection or inference from behavior explains it.
agent_relevance: Moderate, trainable access. Not enough to relax G10.

source: Laine et al. (2024) Me, Myself, and AI: the Situational Awareness Dataset (SAD)
finding: 16 LLMs on a benchmark of self-knowledge, situation inference and self-dependent instruction following. All above chance, none at human level on some tasks. Chat tuning and a situating prompt raise scores.
numbers: Best plain score: Claude 3 Opus 63.2%, Claude 3 Sonnet 62.2%. The situating prompt usually gives a large increase. SAD is only partly predicted by MMLU.
limits: Facts about oneself, not proof of internal access; contamination risk.
agent_relevance: Tell the model its situation in the prompt. That helps more than hoping it knows.

source: Comsa & Shanahan (2025) Does it make sense to speak of introspection in large language models?
finding: A model describing its own creative process is not introspection. A model correctly inferring its sampling temperature is a minimal case, with no consciousness implied.
numbers: Two case studies; no statistics.
limits: Conceptual argument with small examples.
agent_relevance: Self-reports about process are text generation. Self-reports of simple observable parameters can be fine.

source: Nisbett & Wilson (1977) Telling more than we can know
finding: Classic claim: people cannot report the causes of their judgments and instead apply plausible theories. The stocking study showed a strong position effect that nobody mentioned.
numbers: From memory, not opened: about 52 shoppers; the right-most item chosen about four times as often as the left-most. Verify before citing.
limits: Criticized (Smith & Miller; White; Ericsson & Simon): reports are better when immediate, concurrent and about content rather than cause. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Human origin of G10. Concurrent reports of content may be usable; causal explanations are not.

source: Johansson, Hall et al. (2005) Failure to detect mismatches between intention and outcome in simple decision making (choice blindness)
finding: Participants often did not notice swapped photos and justified the choice they did not make.
numbers: Not opened. Only figure available this session is secondhand: the 2025 paper (b04) says about 13% called out the swap in the classic setting.
limits: Strongly design-dependent. Reinterpreted by the covert-detection account in b04.
agent_relevance: Confabulation exists but its rate depends on setup. Expect context-sensitive self-report in agents too.

source: Maniscalco & Lau (2012) A signal detection theoretic approach for estimating metacognitive sensitivity from confidence ratings
finding: Introduced meta-d' and M-ratio (meta-d' divided by d') to compare metacognitive sensitivity across levels of task performance.
numbers: Seen only as a citation inside b01 and b02.
limits: b02 finds M-ratio mostly independent of task performance but with poor test-retest reliability.
agent_relevance: Score the agent's confidence by discrimination (meta-d' style), not raw hit rate of confident answers.

source: Lindsey (2025) Emergent introspective awareness in large language models (Anthropic)
finding: Concept vectors injected into activations; the model is asked whether it notices something. Best models sometimes detect and name the concept, but rarely.
numbers: Not opened. From memory: best models detect on the order of 20% of trials with few false positives. Verify before citing.
limits: Unopened, numbers uncertain. Described as sensitive to prompt and layer, unreliable on most trials.
agent_relevance: Real but rare internal access. Reinforces: never depend on it.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What large language models know and what people think they know (Nat Mach Intell)
finding: Users overestimate LLM accuracy when explanations are long. Matching explanation length to model confidence narrows the calibration gap.
numbers: Not opened; numbers not recorded.
limits: Unopened.
agent_relevance: Explanation length inflates trust. Strip decorative reasoning before a downstream judge sees confidence.
